blocks.title: Beats
blocks.text: When two waves of slightly different frequencies, travelling in the same direction, overlap each other, there is a periodic variation of sound between maximum and minimum loudness, which is called beats.

Tuning forks give out pure notes (a single frequency). If two tuning forks A and B of the same frequency, say 32 Hz, are sounded separately they give out pure notes; sounded simultaneously, it is difficult to differentiate the note of one fork from that of the other, as their sound waves superpose and are heard as a single pure note. If fork B is loaded with some wax or plasticine, its frequency is lowered slightly, say to 28 Hz; now if the two forks are sounded together, a note of alternately increasing and decreasing intensity is heard. This note is called a beat note, or a beat, and is due to interference between the sound waves from forks A and B.

Fig. 7.12(a) shows the waveform of the note emitted by fork A, Fig. 7.12(b) that of fork B, and Fig. 7.12(c) the resultant when both are sounded together; it shows how the beat note occurs. At some instant X the displacements of the two waves are in the same direction, the resultant displacement is large and a loud sound is heard. Later the displacement due to one fork is opposite to that due to the other, giving minimum displacement at Y, so a faint sound or no sound is heard; later again the displacements are in the same direction and a loud sound is heard at Z.

As the difference of the frequencies of the two forks is also 4 Hz, the number of beats per second equals the difference between the frequencies of the tuning forks: fA = 32 Hz, fB = 28 Hz, fA greater than fB, number of beats = fA - fB = 32 Hz - 28 Hz = 4. However, when the difference between the frequencies of the two sounds is more than 10 Hz it becomes difficult to recognise the beats. One can use beats to tune a string instrument such as a piano or violin by beating a note against a note of known frequency; the string is then adjusted to the desired frequency by tightening or loosening it until no beats are heard.

blocks.title: Beat frequency
blocks.text: The difference between the frequencies of the two waves is termed the beat frequency f_beat. If the time interval between two successive loud sounds is T = t2 - t1, then f_beat = 1/T.

blocks.caption: Diffraction, beats and the intensity of a wave (original diagram after Figures 7.11 and 7.12 and topics 7.8 to 7.10).
blocks.long_description: Waves passing a gap comparable to their wavelength spread out widely, while a gap much wider than the wavelength lets them through with little bending. Two notes of slightly different frequency drift in and out of step: when their displacements agree the sound is loud and when they oppose it is faint, so the loudness rises and falls as many times a second as the difference of the two frequencies, here four, and a loud sound is followed by a faint one an eighth of a second later. The intensity of a wave is the power carried through unit area, which for a point source spreads over a sphere of area four pi r squared, and it is proportional to the square of the amplitude.

items: Guitar: playing two strings with slightly different tunings creates beats, for example a standard tuned string and a string tuned a few cents higher or lower.
Piano: playing two adjacent keys, white and black, creates beats.
Violin: playing two strings with slightly different bow pressures or speeds generates beats.
Drums: two drums with slightly different tunings played simultaneously create beats.
Flute: playing two notes with slightly different embouchure (lip and facial muscle) positions generates beats.
Organ: playing two pipes with slightly different tunings creates beats.
Synthesizer: generating two oscillators with slightly different frequencies creates beats.

blocks.text: In each of these examples the slight difference in frequency between the two sound sources creates a periodic increase and decrease in amplitude, a beat or pulsation effect. Musicians often use beats intentionally to create interesting rhythmic effects, add texture, or produce a sense of tension and release; in some cases, however, beats are unwanted and require adjustments to tuning, pitch or playing technique. The sound produced by most string and wind instruments is due to the formation of stationary waves in them (Do You Know).

blocks.title: Example 7.7
blocks.text: Two tuning forks exhibit beats at a beat frequency of 3 Hz. The frequency of one fork is 256 Hz; its frequency is then lowered slightly by adding a bit of wax to one of its prongs, and the two forks then exhibit a beat frequency of 1 Hz. Determine the frequency of the second fork. Solution: f1 = 256 Hz, beat frequency before loading 3 Hz, after loading 1 Hz, f2 = ?. As f1 - f2 = +/-n, f2 = f1 +/- n = 256 +/- 3, so f2 = 259 Hz or 253 Hz. If 259 Hz were correct, loading the first fork would lower its frequency below 256 Hz (255, 254 Hz) and the number of beats would increase above 3. Since the number of beats decreases on loading the first fork, 259 Hz is not the correct frequency; thus f2 = 253 Hz, since 254 - 253 = 1 Hz. In 1711 F. J. Shore, a royal trumpeter and lutenist, invented tuning forks.
